title-group.article-title: A comparative study of Ommaya reservoir versus lumbar puncture for intrathecal chemotherapy in patients with leptomeningeal metastasis: a systematic review and meta-analysis

sec.title: Background
sec.p: Leptomeningeal metastasis (LM) is a lethal complication of advanced malignancy with limited therapeutic options and poor survival. Intrathecal chemotherapy represents a standard treatment for LM and can be administered via repeated lumbar puncture (LP) or an intraventricular Ommaya reservoir. However, the comparative efficacy and safety of these two administration routes remain unclear. This study aims to compare the clinical outcomes of intrathecal chemotherapy delivered by Ommaya reservoir versus LP in patients with LM, and to provide further evidence for clarifying the advantages of the Ommaya reservoir in clinical practice.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: We systematically searched PubMed, Embase and Web of Science for relevant studies published between 1986 and 2026. Studies directly comparing intrathecal chemotherapy delivered via Ommaya reservoir and LP were included in the meta-analysis. Disease control rate (DCR) was pooled as odds ratios (OR) using a random-effects Mantel–Haenszel model to account for between-study heterogeneity, and overall survival (OS) was pooled as hazard ratios (HR) using the inverse-variance method. Because adverse events (AEs) were incompletely reported in comparative studies, an additional safety analysis including single-arm cohorts was conducted using a binomial generalized linear mixed model (GLMM) with a logit link. Risk of bias was assessed using the ROBINS-I tool.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: A total of four comparative studies with a moderate overall risk of bias were included in our meta-analysis. Three studies contributed data on DCR, and three studies contributed data on OS. The pooled analysis showed no significant difference in DCR between the Ommaya and LP groups (OR 2.03; 95% CI 0.53–7.78, p = 0.30), with moderate heterogeneity (I² = 66%). In contrast, Ommaya-based intraventricular delivery was associated with significantly improved OS compared with LP (HR 0.39; 95% CI, 0.25–0.61, p < 0.0001), with no significant heterogeneity (I² = 0%). In the exploratory safety analysis of six single-arm cohorts, the estimated probability of overall AEs was numerically lower in the Ommaya group (OR 0.43; 95% CI, 0.21–0.87, p = 0.0191). While this finding is derived from non-comparative data and should be treated cautiously, it offers valuable insight into safety profile.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Ommaya reservoir–based intraventricular administration of intrathecal chemotherapy may provide a survival advantage over LP in patients with LM, while demonstrating a generally acceptable and manageable safety profile. Further comparative studies with standardized response criteria and rigorous safety reporting are warranted.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Leptomeningeal metastasis (LM) is a lethal complication of advanced cancer, defined by the spread of malignant cells to the leptomeninges and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). LM occurs in patients with metastatic solid tumors or hematologic cancers, especially in those with breast cancer, lung cancer, or melanoma [1, 2]. The diagnosis of LM is based on a comprehensive assessment of clinical presentation, neuroimaging findings, and CSF examination, while CSF cytology remains the gold standard [3]. Representative radiographic and cytological features of LM are presented in Fig. 1. LM often presents with multifocal neurologic symptoms due to neuroaxis infiltration or raised intracranial pressure. Common manifestations include cranial neuropathies, headache, nausea, mental status changes, and spinal/cauda equina symptoms [4, 5]. Even with interventions, outcomes remain dismal, and there is no established standard of care for LM. Management is generally palliative and multidisciplinary, often including radiotherapy to symptomatic sites, systemic therapy targeted at the primary tumor, and intrathecal chemotherapy to directly treat leptomeningeal disease [2, 6]. Given the rarity and lethality of LM, optimizing treatment strategies, especially intrathecal chemotherapy, to improve neurological outcomes and prolong survival is a pressing clinical challenge.

caption.p: Representative radiologic and cytologic findings of leptomeningeal metastasis. (A) Contrast-enhanced brain magnetic resonance imaging showing typical sulcal linear enhancement, suggestive of leptomeningeal involvement. (B) Cerebrospinal fluid cytology demonstrating malignant tumor cells

sec.p: Intrathecal chemotherapy is a key component of LM treatment, designed to bypass the blood–brain barrier to achieve therapeutic drug levels in the CSF [7]. Intrathecal therapy can be administered by two principal routes: repeated lumbar puncture (LP) injections into CSF, or via an Ommaya reservoir – a surgically implanted intraventricular catheter system that allows direct drug delivery into the lateral ventricle (schematically illustrated in Fig. 2). Mechanistically, drug distribution within the subarachnoid space is heavily dependent on CSF bulk flow dynamics. Because physiological CSF flows predominantly in a rostro-caudal direction from the ventricles to the spinal subarachnoid space, intraventricular administration via an Ommaya reservoir can theoretically provide a more uniform and predictable drug distribution throughout the neuroaxis. In contrast, drugs injected via lumbar puncture must diffuse against this physiological gradient, often resulting in incomplete distribution and limited therapeutic concentrations in the cranial compartments. Current evidence suggests that the use of an Ommaya reservoir may confer advantages in terms of treatment efficacy and prognosis [8, 9]. However, most existing data are derived from single-center, small-sample observational studies, leading to inconsistent conclusions and a lack of high-quality evidence to guide clinical practice. To fill this evidence gap and provide evidence-based support, we systematically synthesized the available data, aiming to determine which intrathecal delivery approach offers a significant advantage in prolonging survival or achieving CSF disease control. Clarifying the relative benefits and limitations of intraventricular chemotherapy via an Ommaya reservoir versus intrathecal chemotherapy via LP will provide valuable evidence to guide clinical decision-making and may help optimize treatment strategies for patients suffering from this challenging and lethal complication of cancer.

sec.title: Search strategy
sec.p: Overall, this systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted and reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines (see PRISMA checklist in Supplementary Metarials) [10]. We conducted a systematic search of PubMed, Web of Science and Embase for relevant literature between 1986 and 2026. A comprehensive literature search was conducted to retrieve all eligible published and unpublished primary studies. The following Boolean search string was used in PubMed search: (“leptomeningeal metastasis“[Title/Abstract] OR “meningeal carcinomatosis“[Title/Abstract] OR “leptomeningeal carcinomatosis“[Title/Abstract]) AND (1986:2026[pdat]). The final search was conducted on March 30, 2026. Equivalent search terms were adapted for the other databases: ‘leptomeningeal metastasis’, ‘meningeal carcinomatosis’, ‘leptomeningeal carcinomatosis’. Two reviewers independently screened the titles and abstracts of the retrieved records, followed by a full-text assessment to identify eligible observational studies. Furthermore, the reference lists of all included studies were manually checked to identify additional potentially relevant publications. The search was restricted to human studies and articles published in English.

sec.title: Inclusion/exclusion criteria
sec.p: Studies were considered eligible for inclusion if they met the following criteria: (1) a comparison between intrathecal injection via an Ommaya reservoir and via lumbar puncture; (2) each study arm included 8 or more patients who had undergone chemotherapy in the same center.

The rationale for setting this minimum sample size threshold is grounded in both clinical and statistical considerations. Given the rarity of leptomeningeal metastasis, extremely small case series often reflect anecdotal clinical experiences rather than standardized institutional protocols, making them highly susceptible to extreme selection bias and “small-study effects.” From a statistical perspective, including extremely small cohorts can introduce severe random error, generate unstable variance estimates in the meta-analysis, and compromise the convergence and reliability of the generalized linear mixed model (GLMM) used for adverse event pooling. Therefore, these thresholds were established to ensure a baseline level of institutional experience and to maintain the robustness of the pooled estimates.
The exclusion criteria were as follows: (1) non-investigative studies (case report, letters, and comments); (2) study that did not specify the method of intrathecal injection, non-human studies.

sec.title: Methodological quality
sec.p: The risk of bias of the included non-randomized comparative studies was assessed using the Risk Of Bias In Non-randomized Studies – of Interventions, Version 2 (ROBINS‑I V2) [11]. The risk of bias was assessed independently by two reviewers using the ROBINS-I tool, with disagreements resolved by consensus.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Data extraction was performed independently by two reviewers. Any discrepancies were resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer. Review Manager, version 5.4 was used for the meta-analysis. All outcomes assessed in the present study included dichotomous and time-to-event data; thus, event rates along with their corresponding 95% confidence interval (CI) are presented. We used odds ratio (OR) and hazard ratio (HR) as summary statistics. OR > 1 for DCR favors the Ommaya reservoir, whereas HR < 1 for OS favors Ommaya reservoir.

To ensure methodological transparency, the extraction of HRs for OS was performed according to the following hierarchy: (1) HRs and 95% CIs were extracted directly from the original articles if they were explicitly reported based on multivariate Cox proportional hazard models; (2) If HRs were not directly reported, reported with mathematically inconsistent confidence intervals, or only Kaplan-Meier survival curves were available, the HRs and their variances were indirectly estimated from the published Kaplan-Meier curves or summary statistics (log-rank p-value, median survival, and number of events) using the widely accepted methods described by Tierney et al. [12] and Parmar et al. [13].

For each meta-analysis, heterogeneity was evaluated using the Chi-square test and the I² statistic. A fixed-effects model was employed in the absence of heterogeneity (p > 0.05, I² = 0%) or in cases of minimal heterogeneity (p > 0.05, I² < 25%). Conversely, a random-effects model was adopted when substantial heterogeneity was observed (p < 0.05, I² > 50%). The incidence of adverse events was analyzed using a GLMM with a logit link function, and differences were considered statistically significant if the p value was < 0.05. Formal assessment of publication bias using funnel plots, Harbord-Egger, or Begg-Mazumdar tests was not performed. The number of included comparative studies (n = 4) was well below the standard threshold (n = 10) recommended by the Cochrane Handbook, meaning such tests would lack adequate statistical power to detect meaningful asymmetry. Due to the limited number of included comparative studies (n = 4), formal sensitivity analyses could not be robustly performed either.

sec.title: Study selection and characteristics
sec.p: A comprehensive systematic literature search across PubMed, Web of Science and Embase yielded a total of 6750 records. Initially, 1894 records were removed due to duplication. Based on our predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria, 4811 records were excluded, leaving 45 articles for full-text evaluation. Following a rigorous full-text assessment, 41 articles were further excluded due to non-comparison design, non-investigative study or not specifying injection route. The entire screening process is presented in the PRISMA 2020 flow diagram (Fig. 3). Ultimately, four two-arm studies were identified for the head-to-head comparison of intrathecal chemotherapy delivered via an Ommaya reservoir versus lumbar puncture (LP) [14–17], and the characteristics are listed in Table 1a and 1b. Because outcome reporting was inconsistent across studies, meta-analyses were performed only when a common effect measure could be derived. Accordingly, DCR was pooled as odds ratio (OR) using a random-effects Mantel–Haenszel model due to the presence of heterogeneity, and overall survival (OS) was pooled as hazard ratio (HR) using the inverse-variance approach.

sec.title: Methodological quality and risk of bias
sec.p: The risk of bias for the four non-randomized comparative studies was evaluated using the ROBINS-I tool, and the detailed assessment across all seven domains is summarized in Table 2. Overall, all four included studies were judged to be at a “moderate” risk of bias. Although the allocation to Ommaya reservoir or lumbar puncture was not randomized, the risk of confounding (Domain 1) was considered moderate rather than serious because the included studies either demonstrated comparable baseline characteristics between the two groups or utilized multivariate Cox proportional hazard models to adjust for potential confounders. Other domains, including bias in the classification of interventions, missing data, and measurement of outcomes, were generally rated as “low” risk, given the objective nature of the surgical interventions and the survival endpoints. This indicates a generally acceptable methodological quality of the included evidence.

sec.title: Disease control rate
sec.p: The result of meta-analysis was shown in Fig. 4. DCR was reported in three studies [14, 15, 17]. Given the moderate-to-substantial heterogeneity (Chi² = 5.83, df = 2, p = 0.05; I2= 66%), a random-effects Mantel–Haenszel model was applied in accordance with our prespecified methodological framework. The pooled estimate did not demonstrate a statistically significant difference in DCR between Ommaya and LP administration (OR 2.03; 95% CI, 0.53–7.78, p = 0.3). This indicates that DCR effects were not consistent across studies. Taken together, these data suggest that evidence for superior disease control with Ommaya versus LP remains inconclusive based on available comparative studies, and any apparent differences in individual cohorts should be interpreted cautiously in light of heterogeneity and imprecision.

sec.title: Overall survival
sec.p: Three studies contributed data suitable for time-to-event synthesis as HR [14, 16, 17], and a random-effects inverse-variance model was used to account for potential clinical differences across cohorts and treatment eras. The pooled analysis showed a significant OS benefit favoring Ommaya delivery over LP (HR 0.39; 95% CI, 0.25–0.61, p < 0.001). Statistical heterogeneity was negligible (Tau² = 0.00; Chi² = 1.44, df = 2, p = 0.49; I2 = 0%), supporting the robustness and consistency of the observed survival advantage across the included studies. Consistent with the meta-analytic findings, descriptive medians generally trended toward longer OS in the Ommaya group, though median-based comparisons should be interpreted as supportive rather than definitive given differences in follow-up and censoring.

sec.title: Safety analysis
sec.p: Following the comparative meta-analyses of dual-arm studies, we additionally assessed treatment tolerability using a broader evidence base. Because adverse events (AEs) were sparsely and inconsistently reported in the head-to-head studies, and because several relevant cohorts were available only as single-arm series, we conducted a separate analysis incorporating single-arm data to compare AE risk between administration routes.

There were six single-arm cohorts pooled in our analysis. The characteristics of pooled studies were listed in Table 3. Specifically, two cohorts evaluated intrathecal/intraventricular chemotherapy delivered via an Ommaya reservoir, and four cohorts evaluated delivery via lumbar puncture [18–23]. For each cohort, we extracted the number of AEs and we specifically quantified AEs of grade 3 or higher, to investigate the safety disparities between Ommaya reservoir and lumbar puncture.

sec.p: The model-based predicted probabilities of overall and grade ≥ 3 adverse events according to administration route are shown in Fig. 5. Using a binomial GLMM with a logit link and a study-level random intercept, we compared adverse-event risks between Ommaya administration and lumbar puncture (LP) across studies. For overall adverse events, the model-based predicted probability was 33.3% for Ommaya versus 53.9% for LP, corresponding to an odds ratio (OR) of 0.43 (95% CI 0.21–0.87, p = 0.0191). For grade 3 or higher adverse events, the predicted probability was 4.4% for Ommaya versus 17.2% for LP (OR = 0.22; 95% CI 0.05–0.99, p = 0.0491). Overall, while the point estimates from this exploratory model suggested lower rates of both overall and severe AEs with Ommaya compared with LP, these findings must be interpreted with strict caution. Because the data were derived from non-comparative, single-arm studies, they are highly susceptible to confounding. Substantial difference in patient populations, underlying malignancies, treatment regimens, and AE reporting standard across the included studies preclude any definitive comparative or causal conclusions regarding the safety superiority of Ommaya over LP.

sec.title: Principal findings
sec.p: Leptomeningeal metastasis (LM) remains a devastating complication of advanced cancer, characterized by dissemination of malignant cells within the leptomeninges and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), leading to multifocal neurologic deficits, impaired CSF circulation, and a persistently poor prognosis despite multimodality care. The optimal route of intrathecal administration—repeated lumbar puncture (LP) versus intraventricular delivery via an implanted Ommaya reservoir—is clinically important, because route selection affects feasibility of repeated dosing, monitoring, and potentially drug distribution and efficacy. Recent expert guidance from the EANO–ESMO Clinical Practice Guideline and the Chinese expert consensus explicitly state that intrathecal chemotherapy should be delivered via the ventricular route when possible [24, 25], reflecting both practical and pharmacologic considerations.

In our synthesis of comparative studies, intraventricular administration via an Ommaya reservoir was associated with a statistically significant overall survival (OS) advantage compared with LP (pooled HR = 0.39), with moderate statistical heterogeneity. In contrast, disease control rate (DCR) did not significantly differ between routes (pooled OR = 2.03) and showed moderate-to-substantial heterogeneity. Clinically, these findings suggest that route choice may be more consistently reflected in time-to-event outcomes (OS) than in DCR, and that the survival association observed with Ommaya delivery is unlikely to be driven solely by short-interval ‘disease control’, which is variably defined across studies.

sec.title: Interpretation of survival and disease control findings
sec.p: Several factors may explain why OS appears more sensitive to route than DCR. First, OS is a relatively objective endpoint, whereas DCR in LM can be operationalized in heterogeneous ways (clinical symptoms, MRI interpretation, CSF cytology, or composite measures), assessed at nonuniform time points, and influenced by the intrinsic difficulty of evaluating LM response. This is precisely why the Response Assessment in Neuro-Oncology (RANO) LM group proposed standardized response criteria and an MRI scorecard, acknowledging that most LM lesions are nonmeasurable and imaging assessment can be subjective [26]. Second, OS integrates downstream benefits that may not be captured by early DCR, including sustained treatment delivery, fewer interruptions, and improved capacity for longitudinal monitoring and timely escalation of therapy. Third, the observed OS advantage may also be influenced by unmeasured procedure-related factors. Specifically, patients selected for Ommaya reservoir placement often represent a more favorable clinical subset—such as those with better performance status, longer expected survival, or fewer systemic comorbidities—which inherently predisposes them to better outcomes. In some patients, Ommaya reservoir placement may facilitate concomitant CSF drainage interventions, such as ventriculoperitoneal shunting or repeated CSF aspiration, which could relieve intracranial hypertension and improve neurological status. Because such information was not consistently available in the included studies, residual confounding cannot be fully excluded, and prospective studies are needed to confirm whether the OS benefit is truly attributable to the administration route itself.

sec.title: Potential advantages of Ommaya delivery
sec.p: Route-dependent CSF pharmacokinetics and distribution have long been recognized. In a classic study, Shapiro and colleagues examined methotrexate kinetics after intravenous infusion, intraventricular administration via an Ommaya reservoir, and intralumbar injection, demonstrating route-related differences in CSF exposure and distribution patterns and suggesting a potential distribution advantage with Ommaya-based intraventricular delivery [8]. Preclinical and translational data suggest that drug distribution after intralumbar intrathecal dosing may be incomplete and variable, whereas intraventricular delivery (via an Ommaya reservoir) can provide a more controllable and more predictable CSF exposure profile, with ventricular-to-spinal concentration gradients shaped by CSF transport and flow dynamics [27–29].

Beyond pharmacology, Ommaya delivery can improve the feasibility of repeated intrathecal dosing and serial CSF sampling, reducing dependence on repeated LPs that may be limited by patient discomfort, challenging anatomy, thrombocytopenia, procedural delays, or post-dural puncture headache [30]. The practical advantage of reliable access may translate into fewer missed or delayed doses and more consistent monitoring [9] — mechanisms that could plausibly influence OS even when early disease control signals are inconsistent. In real-world cohorts, Ommaya-based access has been reported as safe and feasible for both treatment and frequent disease monitoring in eligible patients [19]. Overall, the low procedural risk of Ommaya reservoir placement, improved patient adherence [19, 29], and the convenience of repeated cerebrospinal fluid monitoring may be important factors contributing to the longer overall survival observed in patients treated via the Ommaya route.

sec.title: Safety considerations
sec.p: Safety is central to route selection, and it is also an area where comparative data are frequently incomplete. To address this, we conducted a separate across-study analysis incorporating six single-arm cohorts (two Ommaya cohorts, four LP cohorts) and compared adverse-event risks between routes using a binomial GLMM (logit link) with a study-level random intercept. This approach was selected to leverage single-arm evidence while partially accounting for between-study heterogeneity.

Although our model-based estimates suggested lower predicted probabilities of AEs with Ommaya administration than with LP, these results are strictly exploratory. The confidence intervals were wide, likely reflecting limited information (few Ommaya cohorts) and heterogeneity across studies. Crucially, as these data originate from non-comparative single-arm studies, we cannot infer a causal or comparative safety advantage for the Ommaya reservoir. The observed differences may be heavily confounded by underlying variations in patient populations, primary malignancies, specific intrathecal and systemic treatment regimens, and institutional standards for adverse event reporting. Therefore, rather than establishing superiority, these findings primarily suggest that Ommaya reservoir placement has an acceptable and manageable safety profile when performed in appropriately selected patients.

However, device- and procedure-related risks of Ommaya reservoir placement should also be considered. In a series of patients with leptomeningeal metastases, placement-related complications were reported in 9.3% of cases, including infection, catheter malposition, and intracranial hemorrhage [29]. In a large 16-year institutional analysis of 616 patients, Ommaya reservoir infection occurred in 5.5% of patients, highlighting infection as one of the most clinically relevant device-related complications [31]. Overall, these data suggest that Ommaya placement is associated with a non-negligible but generally acceptable procedural risk in appropriately selected patients. Therefore, although the potential survival and treatment-delivery advantages of ventricular access remain important, the decision to use an Ommaya reservoir should still take into account neurosurgical expertise, peri-procedural management, and the patient’s bleeding and infection risk profile [24, 32].

sec.title: Clinical implications
sec.p: Taken together, our results support a pragmatic, clinically oriented inference: for LM patients who are candidates for neurosurgical implantation and who are expected to require repeated intra-CSF dosing and frequent CSF monitoring, intraventricular delivery via an Ommaya reservoir is a reasonable — and often preferable — route, consistent with EANO–ESMO guidance. Nonetheless, route selection should remain individualized, incorporating performance status, anticipated survival, platelet/coagulation status, hydrocephalus and CSF flow patterns, burden of systemic disease, concomitant radiotherapy/systemic therapies, and patient preference.

sec.title: Strengths and limitations
sec.p: A key strength of this work is its route-focused synthesis using appropriate effect measures for each endpoint (OR for DCR and HR for OS), combined with a model-based tolerability analysis that explicitly incorporates between-study variability. However, our limitations are substantial. First, the comparative evidence base remains small, and the sample size is limited, which also precluded the formal assessment of publication bias. Second, there is considerable clinical and methodological heterogeneity among the included studies. Pooling data across diverse primary tumor types, varying intrathecal and systemic treatment regimens, and different treatment eras introduces substantial variability. This heterogeneity could significantly confound both survival and safety outcomes. For instance, the evolution of highly effective systemic targeted therapies and improvements in supportive care over the past decades may independently prolong survival and alter adverse event profiles, irrespective of the intrathecal administration route [33]. Third, selection bias is a major concern. Patients undergoing Ommaya reservoir placement likely represent a more favorable clinical subset, which may lead to an overestimation of the survival advantage associated with intraventricular delivery. DCR heterogeneity further limits certainty and reinforces the need for standardized endpoints and adoption of RANO LM response criteria in future trials [26].

sec.title: Future directions
sec.p: Future research should prioritize prospective, multi-center designs that better isolate the effect of route from confounding — potentially via pragmatic trials, or robust observational methods such as target-trial emulation and propensity-based approaches. Studies should standardize (1) route-specific technique (including intraventricular injection protocols), (2) response endpoints (RANO LM criteria), (3) CSF flow assessment strategies, and (4) comprehensive device-related complication reporting. Finally, given ongoing debate about the role and optimal integration of intrathecal therapy in the era of effective systemic agents, balanced appraisals of indications and patient selection remain critical [7].

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: In summary, our comparative analysis suggests a potential association between Ommaya-based intraventricular delivery of intrathecal chemotherapy and improved OS compared with LP; however, this conclusion should be considered cautiously due to selection bias in the non-randomized studies, while evidence for superior DCR remains inconclusive and heterogeneous. A complementary single-arm, across-study analysis indicated an acceptable safety profile for Ommaya delivery, though definitive comparative conclusions cannot be drawn due to inherent study heterogeneity. These findings reinforce guideline-consistent consideration of intraventricular delivery for eligible patients requiring repeated intrathecal therapy, and they highlight the need for prospective, standardized studies integrating CSF flow dynamics, modern systemic therapy backbones, and rigorous safety reporting.
